new_entities.name: High ferritin
new_entities.description: Serum ferritin levels above the person's lower-risk baseline range, often reflecting higher iron stores or inflammation.

edges.effect_quant: Across a 3-year cohort of 575 normoglycemic men, higher baseline ferritin tertiles predicted significantly higher HOMA-IR at follow-up.
edges.population: adults without overt iron-overload disorders, especially men and postmenopausal women
edges.mechanism: Higher ferritin may reflect greater stored iron, which can intensify oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and hepatic or adipose insulin-signaling dysfunction. The biology is not purely causal because ferritin also tracks inflammation, but the association is repeatedly observed in metabolic cohorts.
edges.summary: Elevated ferritin is repeatedly associated with worse insulin sensitivity, although the relationship is not as clean as a direct toxic exposure because ferritin can also move with inflammation and liver injury. The best evidence supports a cautious harmful or risk-marker interpretation rather than claiming ferritin alone causes insulin resistance in every setting.
edges.caveats: Ferritin is an imperfect proxy for total-body iron and rises with inflammation, alcohol use, fatty liver, and metabolic syndrome itself. This edge should be read as a modest adverse signal or marker-level association, not as proof that ferritin lowering alone will reverse insulin resistance.

evidence.citation: Nakamura K et al 2017 Exp Clin Endocrinol Diabetes
evidence.notes: Serum Ferritin, Insulin Resistance, and beta-cell Dysfunction: A Prospective Study in Normoglycemic Japanese Men.

evidence.citation: Fumeron F et al 2006 Diabetes Care
evidence.notes: Ferritin and transferrin are both predictive of the onset of hyperglycemia in men and women over 3 years: the data from an epidemiological study on the Insulin Resistance Syndrome (DESIR) study.

evidence.citation: Gao X et al 2018 Br J Nutr
evidence.notes: Serum ferritin levels are associated with insulin resistance in Chinese men and post-menopausal women: the Shanghai Changfeng study.
